INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

This is an application for
judicial review of the decision of the Professional Conduct Appeal Committee
(the “Appeal Committee”) of the Alberta Teachers’ Association (the “ATA”)
upholding an earlier decision of a hearing committee of the ATA who found the
applicant, Ingrid M. Eggertson, guilty of unprofessional conduct.

BACKGROUND

[
2
]

Ms. Eggertson is a member of the
ATA who has been teaching for the Calgary Public Board of Education since 1977.
She is the mother of two school aged children, Christopher and Carin, who at
the material time, were age 8 (grade 3) and age 6 (grade 2) and in attendance
at the University Elementary School.

[
3
]

On September 26, 1997 during a
“meet the teacher” night it was alleged that Ms. Eggertson made comments
critical of two teachers to the children’s then teacher Ms. Lynda
Campbell-Davies and repeated those or similar comments at a subsequent meeting
on October 9, 1997, which meeting was attended by Ms. Campbell-Davies, another
teacher, and Ms. Anderson, the school principal Mrs. Murtch, and Mr. and Ms.
Eggertson.

[
4
]

The statements which Ms. Eggertson
was alleged to have made were to the effect that: “My children didn’t learn
anything with those two last year” and “Nothing had happened for Christopher’s
learning in that room last year”.

[
5
]

The ATA has established a Code of
Professional Conduct (“the Code”) which provides that a teacher may criticize
the professional competence or professional reputation of another teacher, but
only in confidence to “proper officials” and only after the other teacher has
been informed of the criticism.

[
6
]

Ms. Campbell-Davies was not a
“proper official” nor were Ms. Anderson or Mrs. Murtch. Further, the teachers
to whom the comments were allegedly directed had not been informed of the
criticism.

[
7
]

Ms. Eggertson denies having made
those comments or any similar comments. Her husband, who was in attendance with
her at both meetings, denied that any such comments were made. It was not until
February 17, 1998 that Ms. Campbell-Davies wrote a letter of complaint to the
ATA. That complaint appeared to be based primarily on what Ms. Campbell-Davies
considered to be parental harassment by Mr. and Ms. Eggertson as against Mr.
Campbell-Davies.

[
8
]

An investigation was conducted by
that ATA and Ms. Eggertson was eventually charged with four separate counts.
During the course of the investigation and prior to the hearing, Mr. Stapon, on
behalf of Ms. Eggertson requested among other things, copies of all of the
investigator’s notes. Some of the notes, but not all of the notes, were
provided to Ms. Eggertson. In addition, “will say” statements were provided.

[
9
]

Prior to the hearing, which took
place on January 12, 2000, two of the charges were withdrawn. At that hearing
Ms. Campbell-Davies, Ms. Anderson, Ms. Fraser (the investigator) and Ms.
Eggertson and her husband gave evidence. At the conclusion of the hearing, Ms.
Eggertson was convicted of unprofessional conduct, contrary to the
Teaching
Profession Act
in that she made comments critical to teachers, L. Androsoff
and J. Murtag to Ms. Campbell-Davies who was not a proper official. Ms.
Eggertson received a written reprimand as a result of her conviction. An appeal
of that finding was made to the Professional Conduct Appeal Committee of the
ATA. The Appeal Committee upheld the decision of the hearing committee. It
found no error in judgment by the hearing committee. It was also of the view
that sufficient particulars had been provided to Ms. Eggertson in order for her
to understand the nature and details of the charges against her and to allow
her to prepare for her defence. Ms. Eggertson now seeks judicial review of that
decision.

ISSUES

[
10
]

There are four issues in this
matter:

1.         What is the standard of review that this
Court should apply in this matter?

2.         If the alleged statements were made, should
they constitute unprofessional conduct?

3.         What impact does the failure to produce the
investigator’s notes have?

4.         Is the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
applicable and if so, has it been breached?

DECISION

1.
Appropriate Standard of Review

[
11
]

The appropriate standard of review
with respect to a decision by a statutory tribunal depends upon a number of
factors, such as whether there is a privitive clause, the nature of that
clause, the expertise of the tribunal involved, the purpose of the Act and the
particular provisions being scrutinized, and whether the matter considered by
the tribunal is a question of fact or law. (
Pushpanathan v. Canada

(1998)
1998 CanLII 778 (SCC)
,
160 D.L.R. (4
th
) 193 (S.C.C.)
).

[
12
]

A privitive clause is a statutory
provision which purports to exclude the jurisdiction of a superior court to
review the legality of actions taken by a statutory body. (
Jones and de
Villars, Principals of Administrative Law
, 3
rd
Ed., Carswell,
page 692). Where there is a “full” privitive clause, that is one which declares
that decisions of the tribunal are final and conclusive, and from which no
appeals lies and all forms of judicial review are excluded, the courts will
generally grant a high degree of deference to the tribunal. (
Jones and de
Villars
, page 696).

[
13
]

In this case, we do not have a
“full” privitive clause. While there is no right of appeal, there is
acknowledged to be a right of judicial review. (See Section 56 of the
Teaching
Profession Act
,
Chapter T-3
, R.S.A. 1980 (“the Act”)). I agree with the
respondent’s submissions that there is a demonstrated legislative intent of
limited intervention by the courts in the disciplinary process under the Act,
because of there being no right of appeal set forth.

[
14
]

We next look to the purpose of the
Act in this case, which is to set up an association to deal with matters
affecting the teaching profession (See Section 3(1) of the Act), and the
purpose of the disciplinary provisions in particular, which is to create a process
to consider and deal with the conduct of teachers.

[
15
]

We then look to the nature and
expertise of the members of the hearing committee and the appeal committee. In
this case, these committees are comprised of members of the teaching profession
who are called upon to determine whether any particular conduct is
unprofessional. The hearing committee in this case determined whether a certain
conduct did in fact take place. If it did, it was required to determine whether
that conduct was critical of the professional competence or reputation of
another teacher.

[
16
]

There is no particular expertise
required to determine whether certain events did or did not take place, but a
hearing committee is certainly as qualified as a jury in a criminal case to
make that determination of fact. Whether the conduct in question was or was not
unprofessional is something which teachers are uniquely qualified to deal with.
They are the people who are trained and experienced in what is involved in
teaching. They know what is and what is not or may not be conducive to the
carrying out of their duties as teachers. They know what the standards are and
ought to be.

[
17
]

Bastarache, J.
in
Pushpanathan
,
at paragraph
32
; confirmed that expertise was, “the most important of the
factors that a Court must consider in settling on a standard of review”. He
went on to say:

If
a tribunal has been constituted with particular expertise with respect to
achieving the names of the an Act, whether because of the specialized knowledge
of its decision-makers, special procedure or non-judicial means of implementing
the Act, the greater degree of deference will be accorded.

In my respectful view, this
is particularly applicable in this case.

[
18
]

Finally, we turn to whether the
matter determined by the hearing committee was a question of fact or law. The
answer, of course, is that it was both. Whether the alleged statements were
made, and whether they constituted criticisms which would amount to unprofessional
conduct, were questions of fact. Whether there was adequate disclosure was a
question of fact and law. Whether the
Charter
applied was purely a
question of law.

[
19
]

In the end result, in view of the
nature of the hearing and the issues raised, it seems to me that there are
really two standards of review applicable in this case. There is a privitive
clause but it is not a “full” privitive clause. The hearing committee did have
the expertise to deal with the principle issue before it, that is what was said
and whether any comments found to have been made did constitute criticism of a
teacher and were therefore unprofessional. Further, the hearing committee was
acting in accordance with the purpose of the Act. These factors weigh heavily
toward a patently unreasonable standard. At the very least, they weigh towards
a reasonableness standard, such that my focus should be, not upon whether I
agree with the findings of the committee, but whether there was a reasonable
basis for its decision.

[
20
]

It is that standard which I shall
apply to the factual part of the hearing committees decision. On the issues of
whether there was proper disclosure and whether the
Charter
was
applicable, I will then apply the standard of correctness, as those issues were
mixed fact and law and pure law.

2.
Unprofessional Conduct

[
21
]

A fair amount of Ms. Eggertson’s
application dealt with how the complaint came to be made, the investigation and
the hearing itself. It was strenuously argued that the evidence simply did not
support a finding that the statements were made. It was also argued that even
if those statements were made, Ms. Eggertson had the right to do so as she was
speaking, not as a teacher, but as a concerned parent. When one considers the
nature of the statements and the relative obscurity and privacy of the venue in
which they were made, they were not or should not have been sufficient to
warrant a finding of unprofessional conduct.

[
22
]

Let me say firstly that it appears
to me that Ms. Campbell-Davies initial focus was not so much on any criticism
that may have been levelled against the two previous teachers of Ms.
Eggertson’s children, but at her. Let me also say that I have some difficulty
with how the proceedings initially unravelled. Having said that, Ms. Eggertson
was represented at the hearing by extremely competent counsel. All of the
arguments made before me were made before the hearing committee. Ms.
Campbell-Davies and Ms. Anderson were, I am sure, subjected to intensive
cross-examination. The hearing committee had the task of listening to all of
the evidence presented and assessing the credibility of the witnesses. They had
the benefit of being able to observe the witnesses. The members of that
committee were in a far better position than I to assess credibility. Their
finding was not perverse. There was a reasonable basis for it. Whether I would
or would not have made the same finding is not the point. It was the
committee’s duty to conduct a fair hearing and make a decision based upon all
of the evidence before them and the arguments made to them. There is nothing
before me which would suggest the hearing was not a fair one (subject to the
arguments to be made further in this matter). There were adequate grounds upon
which they based their decision. It is not open to this Court to disturb that
decision.

[
23
]

Having made that finding, it must
now be determined whether the committee’s further findings that those
statements were a criticism of the two teachers did constitute unprofessional
conduct were reasonable decisions. In my view they were. Although
unprofessional conduct is usually related to professional activities, it can
also encompass conduct unrelated to an individual’s professional duties.

[
24
]

In
Ross v. New Brunswick School
District No. 15
,
1996 CanLII 237 (SCC)
,
[1996] 1 S.C.R. 825
, the Supreme Court of Canada noted
that teachers may wear their teaching hats off duty. At page 857, LaForest, J.,
stated that “the conduct of a teacher is evaluated on the basis of his or her
position, rather than whether the conduct occurs within the classroom.” In

Re: Cromer v. British Columbia’s Teachers Federation

(1986),
1986 CanLII 143 (BC CA)
,
29 D.L.R. (4
th
)
641
, the British Columbia Court of Appeal rejected the appellant teacher’s
argument that the code of ethics did not apply to the time she made impugned
statements since she was speaking at an adjourned meeting of a Parents Advisory
Committee. Lambert, J.A., writing for the Court, stated, at page 660:

I
do not think that people are free to choose which hat they will wear on what
occasion. Mrs. Cromer does not always speak as a teacher, nor does she always
speak as a parent, but she always speaks as Mrs. Cromer. The perception of her
by her audience will depend on their knowledge of her training, her skills, her
experience, and her occupation, among other things. The impact of what she says
will depend on the content of what she says and the occasion on which she says
it.

[
25
]

Ms. Eggertson is not and was not
prevented from advocating on her child’s behalf as a parent. However, as a
teacher, she must do so without violating the Code, which sets out the
appropriate procedure which a teacher must follow when making criticisms
against fellow teachers. The fact that her status as an experienced teacher
provides enhanced impact to any criticisms she may make against other teachers
highlights the importance of the criticism procedures set out in the Code.

[
26
]

Ms. Eggertson argued that the
impugned statements could not reasonably be construed as criticisms of the
professional competence or professional reputation of other teachers. I am
satisfied that, given the expertise and experience of the members of the hearing
committee, there was a reasonable basis upon which that committee came to its
decision that the comments did constitute criticisms of other teachers and did
amount to unprofessional conduct. I agree that the comments were not
particularly offensive, but again, I defer to the expertise of the hearing
committee in that regard.

3.         Failure to Disclose

[
27
]

Ms. Eggertson argues that under
Section 32(2) of the Act, the executive secretary was required to produce the
complete file of the investigator, Susan Fisher, when she requested, in
writing, that Ms. Fraser’s evidence and the notes which she prepared with
respect to witnesses interviewed by her be produced. Both the hearing committee
and the appeal committee refused to order production of Ms. Fraser’s complete
file. They were satisfied that the level and degree of the particulars
submitted by them gave Ms. Eggertson more than adequate notice of the nature
and details of the charges and allowed her to prepare for her defence.

[
28
]

The relevant sections of the Act
are Section 30(3) and Section 37(1), which provide:

30(3)
At least 15 days before the date set for the hearing, the executive secretary
shall serve on the investigated person a notice stating ....

(b)
reasonable particulars of the matter to be heard.

37(1)
The attendance of witnesses before a hearing committee and the production of
records may be enforced by a notice issued by the executive secretary requiring
the witness to attend and stating the date, time and location at which the witnesses
to attend and the records, if any, that the witness is required to produce.

(2)
On the written request of the investigated person or that person’s counsel or
agent, the executive secretary shall, without charge, issue and deliver to that
person or his counsel or agent any notices that the person requires for the
attendance of witnesses or the production of any record.

[
29
]

Pursuant to Section 30(3) Ms.
Eggertson was entitled to reasonable particulars of the matter to be heard and
determined at the hearing. There was no requirement under that section that she
be given all of the evidence to be relied upon by the ATA. There was a duty to
provide her with sufficient information to enable her to make a full defence of
the case to be met.  Section 37, in turn, addresses the issuance of notices to
attend to ensure all necessary witnesses and documents are available for the
hearing before the committee. It does not, in my respectful view, speak to
pre-hearing disclosure obligations or the requirement to produce all records in
advance.

[
30
]

What must now be determined is
whether the common law requires a full and complete disclosure of the ATA’s
documentation. In my view, it does not. In two decisions of this Court  it has
been decided that what we have come to refer to as the “
Stinchcombe

level of disclosure” is not applicable to disciplinary proceedings such as
this.
In
Kullman v. Borbridge

(1995),
1995 CanLII 18109 (AB QB)
,
168 A.R. 227
, Perras, J. held that
two police officers who were facing internal disciplinary matters were entitled
to be dealt with fairly, but did not require the disclosure as contemplated by
Stinchcombe

be provided as there was no criminal stigma attached to a disciplinary hearing.
In
Anderson v. Twin River School District

(1994),
1994 CanLII 8981 (AB QB)
,
25 Admin.L.R. (2
nd
)
20
, Murray, J. held that the duty of fairness (which is required) did not
involve full and complete disclosure.

[
31
]

In this case, Ms. Eggertson was
provided with formal witness statements, summaries of Ms. Fraser’s interviews,
the original letter of complaint and Ms. Fraser’s report. Ms. Eggertson has not
shown that she was prejudiced in any manner by reason of not having received
the full contents of Ms. Fraser’s file. Although Ms. Eggertson did request a
copy of the notes of the interview with the principal and was not provided with
them, she was told that the principal simply had no recollection of the event
and did not wish to be involved. I am satisfied that there was sufficient
disclosure to ensure that she had reasonable particulars of the alleged
wrongful conduct. This was adequate to ensure that she was able to properly
prepare her defence of the charges against her.

4.
Charter of Rights

[
32
]

Ms. Eggertson argues that both the
hearing committee and the appeal committee were wrong at law when they decided
that the statements made by her were not contrary to the freedom of expression
guaranteed pursuant to
Section 2 (b)
of the

Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
. There are conflicting authorities of whether the
Charter

is applicable to a Code of Ethics such as we have in this case. Clearly, as set
forth in
Section 32(1)
of the
Charter
, the
Charter
is to apply to
Parliament and the government of Canada as well as to the legislature and
government of each province. Ms. Eggertson argues that because the by-laws
(i.e. the Code) were passed pursuant to the Act and because Section 8 of the
Act provides that the association may only pass bylaws which are consistent
with other acts or regulations of Alberta, the Code does fall within
“provincial legislation” and therefore cannot be contrary to the provisions of
the
Charter
.

[
33
]

In
Re: Cromer (supra)
, the
British Columbia Court of Appeal appeared to simply assume that the
Charter

did apply to a code of ethics quite similar to that before us. On the other
hand, the Ontario Court of Appeal in
Tomen v. Federation of Women Teachers
of Ontario
(19900, 78 O.R. (2d) 48 was of the view that the by-laws passed
by that Association or Federation did not fall within the scope of government
action and that the
Charter
was therefore not applicable.

[
34
]

In
Re: Westerlund
(1992)
(unreported decision of the Teaching Profession Appeal Board), a board chaired
by Associate Chief Justice Miller of this Court held that, on the basis of
Stoffman
v. Vancouver General Hospital

(1990),
1990 CanLII 62 (SCC)
,
76 D.L.R. (4
th
) 700
(S.C.C.)
, the Code of Ethics of the ATA were rules and directives of the
internal management and therefore were not within the ambit of the
Charter
.

[
35
]

In my respectful view, the
Charter

is not applicable to the Code of Ethics in this matter because that Code
constitutes directives of internal management. They are not within the scope of
government action. Nevertheless, even if the by-laws are within the scope of
government action and if the
Charter
is applicable, I am of the view
that, as was the case in
Re: Cromer
, the limits of freedom of expression
imposed by the Code are reasonable and justified, given the purpose of the code
for the teaching profession.

[
36
]

There is no doubt but that
statements and criticisms made by teachers during off-duty hours maybe subject
to disciplinary action pursuant to a code of ethics. There also appears to be
little doubt but that so long as the limits placed on the freedom of expression
of a teacher are reasonable and justified, then the
Charter
will not be
infringed, assuming it is applicable. In this case, as in
Re: Cromer
,
there is a vehicle for levelling a criticism against another teacher. All that
is required is that the teacher making the criticism do so to the proper
officials, after the teacher being criticised has been informed of the
criticism. There is thus no prohibition against saying something which might be
considered unprofessional about another teacher. There is simply a requirement
that it be done in a certain manner. As
stated by Lambert, J.A. in
Re:

Cromer
at page 660:

The
Code of Ethics is designed to avoid disharmony among teaching colleagues and to
promote professional standards, all in the interest of creating an environment
where the children being taught will receive the best educational opportunity
possible...[T]he Code of Ethics does not preclude criticism by one teacher of another;
it sets out a procedure for making criticism that is intended to increase the
beneficial effects of the criticism and minimize the harmful effects.

[
37
]

In this case Ms. Eggertson has
attempted to distinguish
Re: Cromer
and
Ross
, (previously
referred to), by arguing that the impugned statements in this case were
innocuous, in contrast to those statements in
Re: Cromer
where a teacher
made inflammatory statements about another teacher at a public meeting and
in
Ross

where a teacher made racist and discriminatory against Jews. While the alleged
statements may indeed be innocuous in comparison, the relative gravity of the
conduct in question should go to the penalty imposed if the member is convicted
of professional misconduct, which she was.

[
38
]

The Code itself does not preclude
criticism, but rather requires that the member being criticised receive fair
notification and that the criticisms be made to the proper officials. The
purpose of Clause 13 is to ensure that criticisms or disagreements amongst
colleagues occur in a professional environment. In my view, this is
demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.

[
39
]

The application by Ms. Eggertson
is dismissed. Counsel may speak to me with respect to costs.

at
Calgary, Alberta

day of
